The profile is therefore not a true cross-section and a ~2× deviation at any one wavelength, such as 601.40 nm, may be instrumental.

The PL is up to ~10² times stronger than the Raman peaks at 601–618 nm. Peak heights above the PL and the line shapes depend on the baseline model. Fano-like dips and asymmetry bias Lorentzian positions and widths by about ±1–3 cm⁻¹ and ~10–30% in area, and the very low-S/N 638.38 and 626.90 nm spectra are not much better.

Sampling is coarse and uneven: 12 points from 579 to 638 nm, with spacing from 3.4 to 35 meV. A resonance narrower than ~10 meV, a separate trion resonance and a double A1g resonance cannot be resolved. I do not claim exciton energies, only the observed plateau and onset.

Peak positions scatter by ~1 cm⁻¹, including the Si line (520.7–522.3 cm⁻¹). The Si line is expected near ~522–523 cm⁻¹ at 4 K from memory (not checked), so there may be an offset of ~1 cm⁻¹, or a spectrometer calibration drift between wavelengths. Do not interpret differences smaller than ~1 cm⁻¹ as strain, temperature or doping effects.

Local laser heating at 0.7 mW through a 0.55 NA objective cannot be excluded from the data, because no Stokes/anti-Stokes pair or thermometer is available. Neither can the effective sample temperature at the laser spot, or its possible change between wavelengths.

The ~480 cm⁻¹ band and the weaker structures at 176, 392, 403, 439 and 445 cm⁻¹ are not assigned. The detected structure at 392–445 cm⁻¹ in the 605–611 nm spectra is at least partly the dips described above and not new modes.
The window starts at ~128–148 cm⁻¹ (edge filter), so the low-frequency interlayer shear/breathing modes (and with them a direct layer-number check) are not accessible.

Layer number is an inference from PL brightness, A1g position and the Si behaviour, not a direct measurement. Few-layer or twisted regions could also show some of this behaviour. The A1g to E′ splitting that is usually used for layer counting cannot be extracted because E′ is blended with 2LA(M).
The literature comparisons are from memory without internet access. Section or figure numbers were not verified; they should be checked against the papers before reuse.
questions_for_user: What was the laser power measured at the sample at each wavelength (not just nominal 0.7 mW), and were different dyes used across 579–638 nm? Without this the resonance profile and the 601.40 nm point cannot be validated.

Is the flake a monolayer (optical contrast, AFM, or PL from a different spot at 532 nm)? This decides whether the PL at ~2.0–2.06 eV is direct-gap emission and whether the resonance is that of a monolayer.
What is the PL spectrum over the full range at a fixed non-resonant excitation (e.g. 532 nm) at 4 K, so that the neutral exciton, trion and defect-bound band energies can be read directly?
Is a back-gate or other doping control available? Gate-dependent PL and Raman would test the n-type interpretation.
What spectrometer resolution and grating were used, and was the spectrometer calibrated with a lamp at each laser wavelength? This sets the ~1 cm⁻¹ position uncertainty.
Can you repeat the measurement with crossed polarisation, which suppresses A1g and separates 2LA(M) from E′(Γ), and add finer wavelength steps at 595–605 nm and above 2.12 eV (below 585 nm)?
citations: Molas, M. R. et al., Raman scattering excitation spectroscopy of monolayer WS2, Sci. Rep. 7, 5036 (2017) — 4 K excitation-wavelength dependence of the WS2 monolayer Raman bands with a tunable laser; figure number not verified.

Berkdemir, A. et al., Identification of individual and few layers of WS2 using Raman spectroscopy, Sci. Rep. 3, 1755 (2013) — room-temperature assignments of 2LA(M), E′/E2g and A1g in WS2; figure/table numbers not verified.
limits: The data cannot give exciton or trion energies, binding energies or a resonance width, because the excitation sampling is too coarse and the PL is clipped by the window and edge filter.
The data cannot separate E′(Γ) from 2LA(M), assign the ~480 cm⁻¹ band, or give a layer number without independent evidence.
The data cannot show strain, doping level or temperature quantitatively. Peak positions are constant within ~1 cm⁻¹, which is about the calibration scatter.
The relative intensities between wavelengths cannot be taken as cross-sections without laser power, absorption and interference corrections.

observations.evidence: The 549.3 cm⁻¹ line in the 638.38 nm spectrum (4767 counts, one pixel, neighbours ~160–200) and the 739.6 cm⁻¹ line at 607.91 nm (8508 counts in one pixel plus 2229 in the next) are single-pixel cosmic-ray hits, not phonons. The step at ~128–148 cm⁻¹ in the low-shift data is the edge filter, so the '146 cm⁻¹ peak' reported by a simple peak finder at 611–626 nm is the filter edge. The window also ends at 600–840 cm⁻¹, which truncates the PL at its low-energy side.

observations.finding: There are asymmetric line shapes and dips next to Raman peaks on the PL background at 601–611 nm. This is probably interference between the discrete phonon and the PL continuum (Fano-like) or interference in the absorption. It biases peak positions and widths from simple Lorentzian fits.
observations.evidence: Visible dips at ~225, ~340, ~392 and ~430 cm⁻¹ in the 605–611 nm spectra, and the A1g peak sits on a step where the PL falls from ~45k to ~33k counts. Lorentzian fits at 611.28 nm give a 355.5 cm⁻¹ and 13 cm⁻¹ FWHM 357-band, and at 601.4 nm give 516.7 cm⁻¹ with FWHM 18 for the Si line. Those values are unreliable, not real shifts.

observations.finding: The 601.40 nm spectrum stands out as a possible narrow feature, but I cannot tell a resonance from a laser or focus artifact.
observations.evidence: The A1g area is 9.4×10⁵ at 2.062 eV versus 4.2×10⁵ at 2.048 eV and 7.9×10⁵ at 2.070 eV, and the PL at fixed emission energy 2.00 eV is 134 versus 52 (605 nm) and 58 (599 nm) kcounts. Both Raman and PL are about a factor of 2 higher together, which is what a power or alignment change would also produce. The 601.40 nm Si line fit is poor (FWHM 18 cm⁻¹), so Si cannot be used to check it.

caveats: Intensities are corrected for spectrometer efficiency only. There is no normalisation to the laser power at each wavelength (a dye laser's power and beam profile change with wavelength and with a dye change), to absorption, or to the SiO2/Si interference at each wavelength (290 nm oxide). The profile is therefore not a true cross-section and a ~2× deviation at any one wavelength, such as 601.40 nm, may be instrumental.

The PL is up to ~10² times stronger than the Raman peaks at 601–618 nm. Peak heights above the PL and the line shapes depend on the baseline model. Fano-like dips and asymmetry bias Lorentzian positions and widths by about ±1–3 cm⁻¹ and ~10–30% in area, and the very low-S/N 638.38 and 626.90 nm spectra are not much better.

Sampling is coarse and uneven: 12 points from 579 to 638 nm, with spacing from 3.4 to 35 meV. A resonance narrower than ~10 meV, a separate trion resonance and a double A1g resonance cannot be resolved. I do not claim exciton energies, only the observed plateau and onset.

Peak positions scatter by ~1 cm⁻¹, including the Si line (520.7–522.3 cm⁻¹). The Si line is expected near ~522–523 cm⁻¹ at 4 K from memory (not checked), so there may be an offset of ~1 cm⁻¹, or a spectrometer calibration drift between wavelengths. Do not interpret differences smaller than ~1 cm⁻¹ as strain, temperature or doping effects.

Local laser heating at 0.7 mW through a 0.55 NA objective cannot be excluded from the data, because no Stokes/anti-Stokes pair or thermometer is available. Neither can the effective sample temperature at the laser spot, or its possible change between wavelengths.

The ~480 cm⁻¹ band and the weaker structures at 176, 392, 403, 439 and 445 cm⁻¹ are not assigned. The detected structure at 392–445 cm⁻¹ in the 605–611 nm spectra is at least partly the dips described above and not new modes.
The window starts at ~128–148 cm⁻¹ (edge filter), so the low-frequency interlayer shear/breathing modes (and with them a direct layer-number check) are not accessible.

Layer number is an inference from PL brightness, A1g position and the Si behaviour, not a direct measurement. Few-layer or twisted regions could also show some of this behaviour. The A1g to E′ splitting that is usually used for layer counting cannot be extracted because E′ is blended with 2LA(M).
The literature comparisons are from memory without internet access. Section or figure numbers were not verified; they should be checked against the papers before reuse.
questions_for_user: What was the laser power measured at the sample at each wavelength (not just nominal 0.7 mW), and were different dyes used across 579–638 nm? Without this the resonance profile and the 601.40 nm point cannot be validated.

Is the flake a monolayer (optical contrast, AFM, or PL from a different spot at 532 nm)? This decides whether the PL at ~2.0–2.06 eV is direct-gap emission and whether the resonance is that of a monolayer.
What is the PL spectrum over the full range at a fixed non-resonant excitation (e.g. 532 nm) at 4 K, so that the neutral exciton, trion and defect-bound band energies can be read directly?
Is a back-gate or other doping control available? Gate-dependent PL and Raman would test the n-type interpretation.
What spectrometer resolution and grating were used, and was the spectrometer calibrated with a lamp at each laser wavelength? This sets the ~1 cm⁻¹ position uncertainty.
Can you repeat the measurement with crossed polarisation, which suppresses A1g and separates 2LA(M) from E′(Γ), and add finer wavelength steps at 595–605 nm and above 2.12 eV (below 585 nm)?

limits: The data cannot give exciton or trion energies, binding energies or a resonance width, because the excitation sampling is too coarse and the PL is clipped by the window and edge filter.
The data cannot separate E′(Γ) from 2LA(M), assign the ~480 cm⁻¹ band, or give a layer number without independent evidence.
The data cannot show strain, doping level or temperature quantitatively. Peak positions are constant within ~1 cm⁻¹, which is about the calibration scatter.
The relative intensities between wavelengths cannot be taken as cross-sections without laser power, absorption and interference corrections.
